client: I've been really anxious about this weekend because my partner wants me to meet their friends for the first time, and I can't stop thinking about it. I keep imagining all these scenarios where they don't like me or think I'm weird or boring. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to make the difference, because the anxiety just feels so physical and real, you know?
therapist: That sounds really exhausting — your mind is running through worst-case scenarios on a loop, and on top of that, your body is carrying the anxiety too, which can make it feel almost impossible to think your way out of it. You're right that the physical piece is real and important, and in CBT we actually work with both — the thoughts *and* those body sensations together. Can you tell me a little more about what those physical feelings are like for you, and when they tend to show up most strongly?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: It's mostly this tight, heavy feeling in my chest, and sometimes my hands get kind of shaky. It tends to hit hardest at night when I'm trying to fall asleep, or randomly during the day when something reminds me the weekend is getting closer. I guess I just don't see how noticing those sensations is going to make them go away — it almost feels like focusing on them would make things worse.
therapist: That chest tightness and the shaky hands at night — your body is really working overtime trying to process this worry, and it makes sense that focusing inward feels risky, like it might open a floodgate. The goal isn't actually to stare at the sensations until they disappear, but more to gently signal to your nervous system that you're safe, rather than accidentally confirming its alarm. What do you think tends to happen when you *do* notice the tightness — do you find yourself trying to push it away, or does your mind start racing with more "what if" thoughts?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, it's both — I try to push it away but then my mind just takes over with all these "what if" thoughts anyway, like what if I say something awkward and everyone goes quiet, or what if my partner realizes I don't fit in with their world. It's like trying to hold back water with my hands. I guess I can see what you mean about signaling safety, but I honestly don't know how I'm supposed to do that when my brain is convinced something bad is actually going to happen.
therapist: That image of trying to hold back water with your hands really captures it — the more you resist, the more it finds a way through, and your brain is genuinely convinced it's protecting you from something real. In CBT, one of the things we work on is gently questioning whether those "what if" thoughts are predictions or facts — because your mind is treating them as certainties, but they're actually just possibilities. What's the evidence you have, from past experiences, that you *don't* fit in or that people tend to find you awkward or boring?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean, I can't think of a specific time where someone outright told me I was boring or weird, but that almost makes it worse in a way — like, how would I even know if people were just being polite? I do have friends, and my partner has been with me for a while so obviously something is working, but my brain just kind of dismisses all of that as luck or them not knowing the "real" me yet. I guess I see what you're trying to do with the evidence thing, but it feels like I could always find a way to explain away the positive stuff.
therapist: You've actually just named something really important in CBT — it's called a "cognitive distortion" where the mind discounts positive evidence and inflates the negative, and the fact that you can see yourself doing it is genuinely a significant step. But I'm also noticing that even as you're working through this logically, there's something that sounds almost a little defeated in how you're describing it, like part of you isn't quite convinced this process can help you. Is there a part of you that worries that even if we challenge these thoughts, the anxiety will just find another way to talk you out of feeling okay?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, honestly that's exactly it — it's like even when I can see the logic, there's this other voice that just says "sure, but this time it's different, this time it's real." I guess I'm a little skeptical that just recognizing the pattern is enough to actually change how I feel in the moment when the anxiety is at its peak. It's not that I think you're wrong, it's more that I've tried to talk myself out of it before and it hasn't really worked, so I'm not sure why this would be different.
therapist: That "sure, but this time it's different" voice is so common with anxiety, and it's actually really smart of you to name that just recognizing a pattern isn't automatically the same as *feeling* differently — you're right, and CBT isn't really about talking yourself out of feelings in the moment, it's more about slowly loosening the grip those thoughts have over time with practice. What you're describing sounds less like skepticism and more like someone who has genuinely tried hard before and been let down, which makes a lot of sense. Can you tell me a little about what "talking yourself out of it" has looked like before — because there might be something important in understanding why those attempts felt like they didn't stick?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Usually it's me lying in bed just repeating to myself "it'll be fine, stop worrying, you're being irrational" — kind of like scolding myself into calming down, which obviously never really works. I think the problem is it always felt like I was just trying to silence the anxiety rather than actually dealing with it, but I didn't really know what "dealing with it" was supposed to look like. And then when it didn't work I'd just feel worse, like I couldn't even manage something as basic as calming my own brain down.
therapist: What you just described — scolding yourself into calm — isn't really coping, it's self-criticism dressed up as a solution, and it makes so much sense that it backfired and left you feeling worse about yourself on top of the anxiety. You've actually put your finger on something really important: there's a big difference between *silencing* a feeling and *responding* to it, and what you were doing alone at night sounds genuinely exhausting and unkind to yourself. I'm curious — when you imagine what it might feel like to actually respond to the anxiety with some curiosity or even compassion rather than frustration, does that feel possible, or does it feel almost too foreign to imagine?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, it feels pretty foreign — like, my instinct when the anxiety shows up is frustration, not curiosity, because it feels like an enemy I need to defeat rather than something I should be sitting with. I think part of me worries that if I'm too compassionate toward it, I'm just giving it permission to stick around and get worse. But I guess I can also see that what I've been doing isn't exactly working either, so maybe there's something to explore there.
therapist: That fear makes a lot of sense — that compassion equals surrender — but actually, what you've been doing by treating anxiety as an enemy to defeat is what's been keeping you locked in that exhausting battle, and compassion is less about welcoming it in and more about stopping the fight that's draining you. I'm also noticing that even as you're finding some openness at the end there, something in how you're speaking sounds a little heavier than your words might suggest — like there's more weight to this than just intellectual uncertainty. What do you think is underneath that — is there something about letting go of the "fight" that feels scary or even like losing a part of how you cope?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think you might be onto something there, because the fighting and the worrying almost feels like I'm doing something, like I'm not just passively letting things go wrong. If I stop bracing for the worst, it's almost like I'm being naive or setting myself up to be blindsided, and that feels scarier than the exhaustion of constantly being on guard. I guess the anxiety has kind of become my way of feeling prepared, even if it's not actually helping me.
therapist: What you just said is really profound — the anxiety isn't just a problem, it's actually been doing a job for you, acting as a kind of shield that makes you feel like you're in control and not caught off guard. And I'm noticing that even as you're articulating this quite clearly, there's something in your voice that sounds more distressed than your words alone might convey, like this realization is landing somewhere deeper than just an intellectual insight. What comes up for you emotionally when you sit with the idea that the thing exhausting you most might also be the thing you've been relying on to feel safe?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: Honestly, sitting with that feels kind of sad, like I'm grieving something a little bit, which is strange because it's not like the anxiety has been good for me. But it's been there for so long that I'm not sure who I am without it, or how I'd even function going into something like this weekend without that constant bracing feeling. It's almost like you're asking me to walk into a room without my armor, and I don't know if I'm ready for that.
therapist: That grief is completely real and valid — you're not mourning the anxiety itself, but the sense of safety and control it gave you, and that's a significant thing to recognize about yourself. What strikes me is that even as you're describing something quite vulnerable and emotional, your voice sounds almost quieter and more settled than I might expect — like part of you has been carrying this awareness for a while and is finally letting it land. I don't think this weekend has to be about removing the armor all at once — what might it look like to just loosen it slightly, and trust that you've built more resilience than the anxiety has been willing to let you see?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I like the idea of loosening it rather than removing it entirely, that actually feels a little more manageable than what I was imagining. But I'm not sure what that would practically look like in the moment when I'm standing there meeting these people and the tightness in my chest starts up — like, what does "loosening the armor" actually mean when your body is already in panic mode? I guess I'm open to trying something, I just need it to feel concrete enough that I can actually hold onto it when things get hard.
therapist: That's a really important question, and it tells me you're genuinely ready to work with this rather than just talk about it — which matters. One concrete thing you can try in that moment is what's sometimes called a "grounding anchor": when the chest tightness starts, instead of fighting it or narrating catastrophe, you just briefly name what's physically true and present — "my feet are on the floor, I can feel my breath, I am here right now" — which gently interrupts the alarm signal without demanding it disappear. Can we think together about what a version of that might sound like in your own words, something that would actually feel like *you* rather than a script you're reciting?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
